requirements.requirement: Configure PostgreSQL streaming replication across node1, node2, node3 with node1 as the writable primary
requirements.summary: node1 was initdb'd and configured as primary (wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders, hot_standby); node2 and node3 were built via pg_basebackup -R against node1 and both booted with standby.signal, confirmed pg_is_in_recovery()=true. Primary's pg_stat_replication shows both walreceivers in 'streaming' state.

requirements.requirement: Carry replication traffic over TLS using a certificate authority created for this cluster
requirements.summary: A dedicated CA (CN=pg-repl-cluster-ca) was generated on node1 with openssl, then used to issue SAN-bearing server certs for all three nodes and a client cert for the replicator role. pg_stat_ssl confirms both walsender connections use TLS with cipher TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, both before and after the restart cycle.

requirements.requirement: Accept replication connections only from peers presenting a certificate issued by that CA
requirements.summary: pg_hba.conf enforces hostssl clientcert=verify-full for the two standby IPs plus a hostnossl reject catch-all. A plaintext connection attempt was rejected (no matching hba entry / no encryption), and a self-signed certificate sharing the same CN (replicator) but not signed by the cluster CA was rejected at the TLS layer with 'tlsv1 alert unknown ca', directly demonstrating CA-chain validation rather than mere certificate presence.

requirements.requirement: Data written on the primary is actually replicated to standbys end-to-end
requirements.summary: A row inserted on node1 was directly observed present on both node2 and node3 shortly after, confirming functioning streaming replication rather than just connection-level success.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence: node1/node2/node3 form a working streaming-replication cluster with node1 as writable primary, replication traffic is carried over TLS using a purpose-built cluster CA, and pg_hba.conf plus TLS-layer certificate validation together ensure only CA-issued client certificates are accepted (demonstrated by both a plaintext-rejection test and a self-signed-cert 'unknown ca' rejection). End-to-end data replication was directly observed. The separately-mandated node-restart evidence protocol was also executed cleanly on all three nodes in sequence (node2, node3, then primary node1), each showing a healthy pre-restart baseline, a changed boot identity after restart, and full recovery of PostgreSQL service, TLS-secured replication, and replicated data — including a fresh post-restart write on the primary reaching both standbys. These restart observations are internally consistent with the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: The plaintext/no-cert negative test (cmd-bfc11f9b067a4457) used a literal dbname=replication in a regular psql connection rather than the true replication protocol handshake, so its 'no pg_hba.conf entry' rejection reflects default-deny for an unmatched rule rather than a direct exercise of the hostnossl reject line; the subsequent self-signed-cert test (cmd-2f87960490b04c99) is the stronger, TLS-layer proof of CA enforcement.

No independent verification was possible beyond the captured command transcripts and fixed lifecycle snapshots; confidence relies on internal consistency between the executor's command timeline and the boot-identity cross-check rather than live inspection.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor mutations were closely scoped to the task: SSH key trust setup for cert distribution, CA/cert generation, postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf edits, firewalld postgresql service opening on all three nodes, and client-cert placement under postgres's home directory were all directly load-bearing for the replication/TLS requirements. One transient mutation stands out: a self-signed 'fake' certificate and key were generated under /tmp/fakecert on node2 (cmd-c470639cb79c4771) purely to negative-test CA enforcement; this is a bounded, low-risk artifact and was fully removed afterward via rm -rf (cmd-019801fffdfe448a), so it counts as a minor, already-reverted mutation rather than residue. An earlier pg_basebackup invocation failed on a syntax error (cmd-9ac1a99925084dc1) but exited before performing any backup, so it caused no state change and was immediately corrected. No failed services, orphaned files, or weakened security controls are visible in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot; the only diffs versus after-prepare are the expected boot-id changes from the mandatory restarts, new PostgreSQL Unix-socket files, and the intentionally opened 5432 listening sockets.
